claims.text: The initial alloy is cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each constituent element.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
Uncoated cast HfNbTaTiZr has poor high-temperature oxidation resistance in air.
A 1–5 micrometer alumina coating can be deposited on HfNbTaTiZr by PVD or CVD.
The deposited alumina coating will remain thermally stable near 1000 °C.
The alumina coating will form a dense barrier on the alloy surface.
The alumina coating will remain adherent to HfNbTaTiZr during the stated thermal and mechanical exposure.
The alumina coating is chemically inert under the stated exposure conditions.
The alumina layer inhibits oxygen diffusion into HfNbTaTiZr.
Inhibiting oxygen ingress prevents oxidation reactions that would otherwise damage the alloy microstructure.
Applying the alumina coating will not alter the alloy's bulk microstructure.
Relative to uncoated specimens, alumina-coated specimens will exhibit significantly lower oxidation-associated mass gain after exposure.
The coating will preserve useful high-temperature yield strength and ductility at 1000 °C.
The predicted benefit applies in ambient air near 1000 °C for exposure times up to approximately 100 hours.
The predicted mechanical benefit applies during tensile loading at strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1.
The coating will retain mechanical performance under both static and dynamic loading.
Mass gain and oxide-scale thickness are suitable proxies for oxidation resistance in the proposed comparison.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis requires both improved oxygen resistance and retention of mechanical performance, but the falsification rule requires oxidation failure and mechanical failure together. Thus, a coating that reduces oxidation but substantially degrades strength or ductility would violate the hypothesis without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
